title: Who pays for the second block?
bodyMd:
Many water utilities bill households under an increasing-block tariff: in each month, the first cubic metres are sold cheaply and every further cubic metre at a higher price. The utility serving the town of Velmora charges €0.80 for each of the first 10 cubic metres a connection uses in a month and €2.40 for each cubic metre beyond that. The case for such a tariff looks straightforward. Essential use, such as drinking, cooking and washing, is cheap; discretionary use, such as filling a pool or watering a lawn, is expensive; and because richer households are assumed to use more water, the tariff is expected to make them pay more for each cubic metre than poorer ones do.

The difficulty is that the tariff is applied to each connection, not to each person. A pensioner living alone in a small house who uses 5 cubic metres in a month pays €4.00. The family of four next door, each of whose members uses only 3 cubic metres, uses 12 cubic metres in total and pays €12.80, an average of about €1.07 per cubic metre against the pensioner's €0.80, although every member of the family uses less water than the pensioner does. In Velmora's older apartment blocks the effect is sharper still, because a single meter often serves an entire building. Twenty households sharing one connection pass the 10-cubic-metre threshold within the first days of the month, and almost all of the water they use is billed at the higher price.

None of this shows that increasing-block tariffs are regressive in general. Where each household has its own meter and household size varies little with income, the tariff does what it promises, and surveys of towns that meet both conditions find the richest fifth of households paying markedly more per cubic metre than the poorest fifth. The problem is narrower: the tariff sorts consumers by how much passes through their connection, and it is fair only to the extent that this tracks income. Where large low-income households or shared meters are common, a utility could keep the block structure but set the size of the cheap first block per resident rather than per connection. That remedy has its own cost, since it requires an accurate and continually updated record of how many people live behind each meter.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about increasing-block water tariffs in the town of Velmora. There is no table, figure or mathematical notation. The passage states these figures in words: the utility charges 0.80 euros for each of the first 10 cubic metres a connection uses in a month and 2.40 euros for each cubic metre beyond that; a pensioner living alone who uses 5 cubic metres in a month pays 4.00 euros; a family of four, each member using 3 cubic metres, uses 12 cubic metres and pays 12.80 euros, an average of about 1.07 euros per cubic metre; in older apartment blocks a single meter can serve twenty households.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set about a general real subject, increasing-block utility tariffs, in our own words. The town, the utility and every figure are invented, and the figures are arithmetically consistent with the stated tariff (5 cubic metres cost 4.00 euros; 12 cubic metres cost 8.00 plus 4.80, that is 12.80 euros). The third paragraph opens with a concession that is easy to mistake for the thesis, and it states two separate conditions under which the tariff works as intended, which the questions use as scope tests. Nothing is quoted or paraphrased from any published article or test item.
